newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire parliament remains closed over protests.
newsitem.headline: Zaire parliament remains closed over protests.

text.p: Zaire's parliament was shut for a second day on Tuesday as militant supporters of Prime Minister Etienne Tshisekedi disrupted lawmakers' plans to remove him.
"No MPs dared show up this morning. Even the MPs who belong to the ruling committees who were called on to meet at ten this morning, didn't turn up," state radio reported at lunchtime.
Parliament was due this week to consider the dismissal of Tshisekedi, who has built up huge popular support for his years of tough opposition to veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko.
Tshisekedi alienated both Mobutu's allies and even his own opposition backers by excluding all but his most loyal followers from a cabinet he announced on his first day in power last week.
The opposition alliance that helped return him to the job from which he was sacked by Mobutu four years ago ganged up with rivals to unseat the prime minister.
But Tshisekedi's fanatical supporters moved in force to pre-empt a parliamentary vote against their hero, battling troops on Monday and frightening off lawmakers.
A group of about 20 youths from Tshisekedi's UDPS party stopped cars outside the parliament building on Tuesday.
Witnesses said they stripped one MP of his trousers and smashed the windscreen of another's car on its way to the parliament building.
About 40 para-military gendarmes sealed off the building by midday, but the hundreds of troops who ringed parliament on Monday to stop protesters entering were not deployed.
Members of Tshisekedi's close entourage said they were preparing a large march for Wednesday when the prime minister intends to establish himself at his offices.
His party has threatened to mobilise supporters until the new government is formally set up in the ministries.
The outgoing cabinet of disgraced prime minister Kengo wa Dondo is still occupying government buildings, but most official business is halted because of the crisis, officials say.
Tshisekedi was appointed after parliament voted out Kengo following persistent charges that he mismanaged the government's war against Laurent Kabila's rebels who took up arms in October.
Instead of stabilising Zaire's chronically unstable government to face the rebels who hold more than a third of the country, Tshisekedi's appointment has compounded the crisis.

The two sides continued peace talks in South Africa. Rebels have advanced, taking the city of Mbuji-Mayi, traditionally the fief of Tshisekedi, who draws much of his popular support from the Baluba ethnic group concentrated in the Kasai region.
"Mr Kabila can arrive in Kinshasa by foot. He will not be resisted," said Mukendi wa Mulumba, Tshisekedi's cabinet aide.
"But we are a reality that he cannot sweep under the carpet. He cannot go against the desires of the people," he told Reuters, referring to Tshisekedi's popular following.
Political analysts in Kinshasa say the political chaos reigning in the capital and the continuing lack of any credible central authority can only serve the interests of the rebels.
